Optimistic initial values

Start every estimate far too high. A purely greedy agent tries an arm, gets a disappointing reward, and its estimate drops below the untried arms. So it tries those next. Optimism makes even a greedy agent explore.

10-armed testbed from Lesson 5. Greedy, constant $\alpha = 0.1$. Bars are $Q(a)$, numbers below are pull counts.

Optimistic greedy vs realistic ε-greedy

Average over 400 bandits of how often each agent picks the best arm (S&B Figure 2.3).

The maths

With constant step size $\alpha$, the update is $Q \leftarrow Q + \alpha(R - Q)$. Rewards in the testbed are mostly between $-3$ and $3$, so starting at $Q_1 = 5$ guarantees disappointment:

$$Q_2 = 5 + 0.1\,(R - 5) = 4.5 + 0.1\,R$$

The pulled arm drops to about 4.5 while the untried arms stay at 5, so greedy moves on. Every arm gets tried before the estimates settle.

From Lesson 7, after $n$ rewards the initial guess still carries weight $(1-\alpha)^n$. That weight is how long the optimism lasts:

$$Q_{n+1} = (1-\alpha)^n Q_1 + \sum_{i=1}^{n} \alpha(1-\alpha)^{n-i} R_i$$

Two limits. The exploration happens only at the start, so it cannot help if the true values change later. And the agent needs a rough idea of the reward scale to pick a high enough $Q_1$.
